idiom_name: value-type assignment (struct + mutating method) with swap(_:_:) as the in-place commit
implementation_notes: Swift structs have value semantics: initialisation, assignment and argument passing each produce an independently modifiable copy, so a mutating method can do all the fallible work on a local value and then assign it to self in one move, which is the idiom with its two dangerous halves removed -- the copy is implicit and the commit is a plain store that cannot fail. swap(_:_:) and the tuple exchange (a, b) = (b, a) are the standard-library commit primitives when two existing values must trade contents, and MutableCollection.swapAt does the same for elements. Reference types get none of this for free: a class must either hold its state in a private copy-on-write box (checking isKnownUniquelyReferenced before mutating the backing store) or expose only immutable stored properties and replace the instance, which is the equivalent of the C++ handle-plus-pimpl form.
pitfalls: A class is a reference type: assigning it shares one object, so the value-semantics guarantee must be rebuilt with a copy-on-write box plus isKnownUniquelyReferenced, and forgetting the uniqueness check either mutates shared state or copies on every access.

The copy-on-write box must not be exposed: handing out the backing reference (or capturing self in an escaping closure) makes the object shared and the next in-place mutation observable through the original.

swap(_:_:) requires non-overlapping, uniquely referenced storage; overlapping accesses or simultaneous access to two inout arguments violate the exclusivity law and are diagnosed (or trap) at run time -- use swapAt for elements of one collection.
Value semantics does not imply the copy is cheap: without COW, assigning a large struct copies it, and an Array already inside a struct is only copied when it is mutated, not before.
